talks.title: Keynote
talks.teaser: Uses the film 2001: A Space Odyssey to examine how AI reshapes threats and the human role in defense.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens with the speaker's early years in security, when the field was a hacker scene around events like DEF CON, and contrasts that with today's industry of large budgets, boards and professional threat actors. It frames the daily work of defenders as making attackers' jobs harder.

The central thread is the 1968 film 2001: A Space Odyssey. The speaker reads the HAL character not as a machine turning evil but as a system given conflicting instructions by people, and draws a parallel to security teams handed contradictory priorities. Other points cover AI as a force that accelerates everything, the view that threat actors use AI the way they have always used new tools, and the move from command-line to graphical to natural-language interfaces. Non-deterministic output is presented as a new source of error, illustrated by a near-miss in which a bad indicator of compromise would have blocked a widely used service.

The closing looks ahead to agentic AI making containment decisions at machine speed and asks who stays in the loop. The speaker argues for keeping human judgment, intuition and personal connection at the center of security work, and for preserving curiosity and the hacker spirit as the field becomes an industry.

talks.title: Keynote
talks.teaser: A veteran security leader shares field stories and argues the community must rethink how it handles AI-era risk.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens with the speaker's background across decades of security operations, a stint as a defender before moving into vendor work, and a series of anecdotes from the field. Stories about legacy network hardware, a root account that stayed active long after its owner left, and a forgotten server kept running by an abandoned project show how stale systems and credentials quietly pile up risk.

The middle section turns to AI. The speaker describes an internal language model that queried HR records when asked who disliked the user, an email-borne instruction that tricked a commercial assistant into leaking access, and exposed secrets such as API keys and publicly readable cloud storage buckets. He argues that tools are being deployed faster than they are secured, and that the industry is repeating mistakes it made with the internet, Bluetooth and early web products.

The closing part calls for defenders to explain risk in plain language, to build tools that non-engineers can use, and to support one another as careers shift. Practitioners should treat agent credentials, secret handling, patching and regression testing as urgent work, and should keep the human side of the profession in view, including the relationships built at conferences.

talks.title: A Peek Behind the Curtain: How A.I. Works
talks.teaser: Explains how modern AI models learn from data, read text, generate images and reason, and where they fail.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by arguing that "artificial intelligence" is too broad a label, since it covers very different tools in the way "computer" covers laptops and an old job title. The speaker narrows the focus to large language models, image and video generators, and reasoning agents, and explains how each one is built.

The middle section follows the pipeline. Training data has to be cleaned, because duplicates, mislabeled records and inconsistent formatting push a model toward poor decision boundaries, and a live demo showed that a partial fix can even reduce performance. Text is split into tokens and mapped into numerical embeddings, with word, character and subword schemes compared on cost and nuance. Training adjusts large numbers of weights, and precision and recall, illustrated with a bowl of marbles, show how results are judged. Temperature and attention shape output, and retrieval tools are presented as a way to curb invented answers. Image generation is shown as gradually turning random noise into a picture, and reinforcement learning is illustrated through reward hacking in a simple game.

The closing discussion covered audience questions on whether to block or sanitize risky prompts, whether AI-generated content should be labeled, and how long prompts should be retained given security and legal exposure. The main takeaway is that a model reflects its data, its reward design and how clearly people state their goals, and that many of these tradeoffs have no single right answer.

talks.title: Untangling Security & Privacy Risks Across Today's AI Tools
talks.teaser: Compares the privacy and security terms of major AI platforms and offers guidance on which enterprise tools suit business use.
talks.summary:
The session opens by framing business adoption of generative AI as a fast-moving space where vendor promises and the details in contracts, compliance documents and data flows can diverge. It separates two paths, buying a licensed AI service or building and hosting a model, and notes that building requires far more time, data work and ongoing upkeep than most organizations expect.

The core of the talk compares Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Claude, Perplexity and DeepSeek, plus the OpenClaw agent tool. For each, the speaker reviews compliance documentation, whether customer data is used for model training, residency and retention options, audit logging, and how the licensing tier changes the answer. A recurring point is that enterprise plans usually bring controls that consumer plans lack. Copilot inherits each user's existing Microsoft 365 permissions, so overshared files become easy to find. DeepSeek is advised against for business use because of its terms, and OpenClaw is described as not ready for enterprise use.

The closing takeaway is a reusable prompt for asking an AI vendor to summarize its privacy and security documentation, built around three questions: is the tool safe for a regulated business, can the vendor be trusted with data, and why choose it over alternatives. The speaker stresses that these answers change quickly, so reviews should be repeated, and that access reviews and ongoing user training matter as much as vendor choice.

talks.title: Swatting Flies With Sledgehammers
talks.teaser: Argues that third-party risk programs should aim for reasonable assurance and trust, and proposes ways to cut assessment effort.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a story about a large financial institution's vendor risk review that cost a small company roughly 500 hours over fifteen months, while the data collected was thin. The speaker uses this to ask why third-party risk work consumes so much time and whether the effort matches the value. He frames the goal as reasonable assurance rather than perfection, and argues that time spent on low-value vendor paperwork is time taken from other security work.

He then traces the practice from procurement checklists in the 1990s through shared assessment questionnaires and successive revisions of control frameworks that keep adding requirements. He reviews four common approaches: independent audits such as SOC 2, security ratings services, standard industry questionnaires, and custom questionnaires. For each he lists strengths and weaknesses. Audits can be superficial or come from weak firms, ratings can produce false positives and opaque scores, and custom questions often duplicate standard ones. He recommends accepting industry standards, asking which questions are essential, and accepting existing artifacts such as penetration test reports. He also suggests lightweight open-source checks of a vendor's public footprint and asking peers who use the same vendors.

He closes by arguing that the business owner owns the risk while security advises on it, and that buyers should document their reasoning and revisit decisions over time. The practical takeaway is a smaller, standards-based process that trades some thoroughness for time to spend on higher-value security work.

talks.title: Hacking Customized IDE Distributions
talks.teaser: Examines how customized IDE distributions can be attacked and where their security weaknesses tend to sit.

talks.title: Initial Access in 2026 - The Power of the Spoken Word
talks.teaser: Explains how red teams combine phone pretexting, spoofed caller ID and self-hosted telephony to gain initial access.
talks.summary:
The speakers argue that initial access has become the hardest stage of an intrusion. MFA is widespread, web application footholds are scarcer, filtered phishing is harder to land, and physical device drops are costly to arrange. A cited incident response report found social engineering in roughly a third of cases, and the talk focuses on voice-based pretexting as a route into networks.

Preparation covers target selection and tooling. Recently hired staff in non-technical roles are preferred because they are less likely to question a help desk call, and contact-lookup services help find numbers. Rigid scripts are discouraged in favor of a flexible outline, and calls are built around a calm help desk persona and a question that makes the target re-examine their own actions. Infrastructure centers on aged, generic .com domains and matching email. Caller ID is the hardest part: prepaid spoofing services stopped letting callers pick numbers, so the speakers ran their own Asterisk phone system over SIP trunks and explained how STIR/SHAKEN attestation levels affect spam labeling.

The talk closes with payload delivery through remote support tools, which the speakers said had been highly effective until recently, and with defensive advice. They recommend conditional access, identity threat detection and response, and security awareness training, while noting that behavioral baselines are hard to get right. The main takeaway is that call-based help desk processes are part of the attack surface and need verification steps that a convincing voice cannot bypass.

talks.title: $52 Million in Cybersecurity Fraud Settlements
talks.teaser: Covers a set of cybersecurity fraud settlements totaling $52 million.

talks.title: Undercover HUMINT Operations Inside the Ransomware Ecosystem
talks.teaser: Maps the initial access broker market behind ransomware, drawing on undercover operations to trace how access gets sold.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at the market that sits between criminal access sellers and ransomware groups, a layer that public research rarely sees. The speaker explains that the presenting team runs undercover personas that buy access from initial access brokers under legal approval, and that many of these offers never appear on public forums. Takedowns of forums were shown to reduce visible listings without stopping sales, because brokers shift to private relationships and messaging channels.

The middle section covers data from these engagements. Pricing for access fell from roughly a thousand dollars per victim in 2023 to around five hundred by 2026, while supply surged in 2025 as automated tooling spread. Most access came from info-stealer logs and password brute forcing, with CVE exploitation a smaller but faster-moving category. Some examples showed exploit-derived access offered within about a week of public disclosure, and others showed sales years after a bug was published. Sellers were also seen moving into infrastructure and tooling sales, and smaller organisations appeared to be a frequent target.

The case study followed a Romanian broker linked to several ransomware brands. Operational slips, including a chat message written in Romanian, helped investigators identify him. He was arrested in 2024 and later pleaded guilty, with a sentence of about five years. The practical takeaway is that human intelligence can help set patching priorities and defensive focus, and that basic password hygiene remains an effective defence against the most common access methods.

talks.title: Empathy, Not Telepathy
talks.teaser: Argues that understanding other people works better through empathy than through assuming you can read their minds.

talks.title: The State of Information Security Today
talks.teaser: Looks back at decades of information security challenges and argues that many core problems have not changed.
talks.summary:
Jeff Man opens with stories from his early career, including government cryptography work in the 1980s and 1990s and one of the first government penetration testing teams. He uses these to set out how the field started, when the job was mostly building firewalls and persuading organisations to take security seriously at all.

He then walks through slides from 1998 that he used when advising companies connecting to the internet. The emphasis was on a holistic program that begins with policy, goals and an understanding of which data is valuable, rather than on buying the best firewall. He argues that many of the same mistakes recur today, such as users clicking links, executives not seeing how security ties to the business, and overreliance on technology. He also questions how the industry uses the terms vulnerability, threat and risk, noting that it concentrates on vulnerabilities while neglecting data classification and the cost trade-offs that risk decisions require.

In closing, he criticises buzzwords and fear-driven marketing, and says compliance often determines what organisations actually do. He names purpose as the missing element alongside people, process and technology. His takeaway for practitioners is to understand why a security measure is needed before buying tools for it, and to keep questioning assumptions.

talks.title: Breaking Tokens: Modern Attacks on OAuth, OIDC, and JWT Auth Flows
talks.teaser: Covers modern attacks on OAuth, OIDC and JWT authentication flows and how they can be abused.

talks.title: Gigawatts & Governance: Data Security Crisis No One Is Talking About
talks.teaser: Explains how data center power and infrastructure ownership shape data security, jurisdiction and governance for security teams.
talks.summary:
Nancy Coblenz, who co-founds a company that builds AI data centers and modular power plants, opens by framing data center growth as a power problem. She contrasts the gigawatt-scale buildouts under way with grid capacity that falls well short of demand, and notes that waiting for a grid connection can take years. Audience polls on local acceptance of new facilities and on which weak points attendees have assessed set the tone for the rest of the session.

The middle section argues that ownership of the physical layer matters for security. Examples range from unexpected devices found during assessments, such as HVAC controllers, badge systems and payment terminals, to legacy control systems at power plants. She contends that where data sits, which laws apply to it, who can compel access to it, where hardware originates and who controls the power supply all determine how much trust a team can place in its environment. Vendor chains that extend several layers beyond the contracted party also get attention.

The close urges practitioners to ask direct questions about where data physically sits and under which jurisdiction, to engage facility owners and utilities, and to bring infrastructure risk into audits and vendor reviews. She links these concerns to geopolitical competition over supply chains and ends with a call for people who understand both threats and the infrastructure beneath them.

talks.title: Troubleshooting: Where Information Meets WTF
talks.teaser: Explains a six-step troubleshooting method and how its ideas apply to work, relationships and everyday life.
talks.summary:
The speaker, an offensive security consultant, argues that much of his job is troubleshooting rather than breaking things, and that the same approach to finding the right information, tools and techniques when something fails also applies to attitude, health, relationships and career. The session opens with a breathing exercise and a short framing of how mainstream culture models frustration and grief poorly.

The core of the talk is a six-step loop: observe, resist, iterate, step away, repeat and profit. Observation means clarifying your motivation and intention and recognising the impact you have on others. Resistance asks how you handle frustration and whether you are willing to ask for help. Iterating means working one step at a time, while stepping away covers breaks such as walking, napping or time-boxing work on a calendar. Repeating returns to unsolved problems, and the final step is reflecting on wins, taking notes and sharing them.

Audience members contributed examples from job hunting past automated filters, workplace conflict and procrastination. The discussion covered how to judge how much discomfort you can tolerate before seeking help, and the risk of learned helplessness when answers are always looked up. The closing takeaway is that feedback from reality is useful, and that the framework transfers to finances, health and gardening.

talks.title: I Called Your AI Agent and It Told Me Everything
talks.teaser: Demonstrates how voice AI agents can be probed and manipulated over phone calls, using a repeatable red-teaming method.
talks.summary:
The talk starts by contrasting text chatbots with voice pipelines, including speech-to-speech models that skip text conversion, and explains why that changes what monitoring can catch. The speaker shows how to tell which kind of system is on the other end of a phone line, and how tone, interruptions and response timing can shift an agent's behavior. A sequence of pre-recorded calls to a simulated bank assistant illustrates the method, which the speaker calls the teapot methodology: start with polite rapport, map the agent's persona and boundaries, test what it refuses, and check what tools it can reach.

The middle section covers the wider attack surface. Caller ID used as an identity check is easy to spoof, DTMF key presses may sit outside the model's view, and retrieval data, user profile fields and conversation history can all carry injected instructions. A live demo shows a profile note overriding an agent's rules. Audio-layer tricks such as sped-up or high-frequency commands are covered, along with error messages that leak internal details and prompts that expose secrets or reasoning tags.

The closing section gives defensive guidance: keep secrets and authorization decisions out of prompts, have tools return redacted data, structure instructions clearly, monitor inputs and outputs, and return generic error messages. The speaker recommends building these negative tests into continuous integration and points to the open-source Voice Goat lab for practice.

talks.title: From OSINT to Detection: Building an Agentic CTI Pipeline
talks.teaser: Shows how an agentic LLM pipeline turns threat intelligence reports into validated Sigma detection rules.
talks.summary:
Detection teams face a constant flood of threat reports, and only a small share contain command lines, registry persistence, or other details worth writing rules for. Andrew Skatoff explains that the steps from finding a useful report to deploying a rule are slow and rely on expertise that lives in analysts' heads, and sets out to automate part of that workflow.

The talk walks through Huntable CTI Studio, an open-source prototype that ingests articles from configured sources and scores them with weighted keyword patterns. A random forest classifier then filters paragraph-sized chunks, and analysts can give it feedback and retrain it. Extraction agents pull artifacts such as command lines, process trees, registry keys, services and scheduled tasks, guided by tightly written prompts designed to fail closed rather than invent content. A generation step produces Sigma rules, validates them with pySigma, and checks novelty by comparing matched fields instead of using embeddings. Every run keeps a full trace, and an evaluation system scores prompt and model changes against gold-standard articles.

A human reviews and approves every rule before anything ships. The main takeaways are design choices rather than the tool itself: cheap deterministic filters ahead of costly LLM stages, narrow low-temperature extraction contracts, structured similarity checks, and auditable traces. The prototype is Windows-focused and not hardened for enterprise use, so it should not be pointed at sensitive intelligence on hostile networks.

talks.title: Unlocking Awareness: Escape Experience made Security Fun
talks.teaser: Shows how a portable escape-room box turned security awareness into a team game for non-technical staff.
talks.summary:
This talk explains how a regional Federal Reserve bank's information security team built a portable "escape room in a box" to make security awareness engaging for staff, many of whom are not technical. The speaker describes the goals behind the project: keep it fun, make it collaborative, avoid requiring prior knowledge, and reach colleagues across branches. The box carried a story in which an AI guards a formula, and players had to prove their security knowledge to open it.

The middle of the talk walks through the puzzles in order. Players sort examples of risky behavior, such as sharing a screen, leaving a laptop unlocked, and ignoring phishing. Later steps include a word search built from definitions, a jigsaw puzzle, a crossword with a transparent overlay, a true-or-false password grid, and a multi-factor step that contrasts something you know with something you have. The last step gives a light introduction to encryption using a simple cipher. Teams divided the work, and the speaker noted that players often found solutions the designers had not planned.

The closing lessons are practical: test the puzzles with pilot groups, make assembly instructions clear, laminate parts so they can be reused, keep groups to four to six people, get leaders to play, and follow up with an email summarizing the key points. The team saw more friendly interaction with colleagues and a strong phishing-test result, though measuring the program's impact more formally remains a goal.

talks.title: AI SOC and Securing your Environment
talks.teaser: Explores how SOC teams can fit AI agents into analysis workflows and the new attack paths automated defenses open.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by asking where AI fits into a security operations center, taking a vendor-neutral view of agentic deployments, managed AI SOC services, and how teams can adapt to a changed threat landscape. The speaker argues AI should enable analysts rather than replace them. One example is a PowerShell script beside an endpoint detection tool that collects logs only when a detection fires and forwards them to a SIEM, avoiding constant ingestion costs.

The middle turns to misuse of the same automation. An attacker who learns which events trigger AI-driven workflows can flood them with noise to inflate token costs or overwhelm a small team. An insider scenario follows, in which a locally run model studies an environment and helps plan an intrusion that existing tools may miss. The talk also weighs outside frontier-model APIs against self-hosted models, notes model poisoning risks, and compares per-token and per-agent vendor pricing.

For practitioners, the recommendations treat AI usage as telemetry. Teams should monitor token consumption, alert on spikes in AI investigation volume, document manual fallbacks for when AI workflows degrade, baseline query behavior by identity role, and restrict what agents can reach through MCP servers. Vetting AI tooling as part of the supply chain is also urged, though the speaker concedes there is no mature verification method yet. Audience questions covered the logging script and local model costs.

talks.title: Secure by Design, Trusted Through Compliance
talks.teaser: Reframes security as risk management, showing how compliance can be built on technical foundations to communicate trust.
talks.summary:
Michael Darling opens by questioning the divide between technical security teams and governance, risk and compliance staff. He argues both should aim at the same outcome: reducing the chance that a material impact hits the organization. In his framing, security is risk management that enables the business rather than a department that says no.

The core of the talk is a structured model. Governance comes first, defining decision makers, stakeholders and executive oversight. Risk framing follows, covering legal and contractual constraints, the threat actors targeting the industry, and what different failures would cost. Technical baselines such as CIS benchmarks or NIST 800-53 come next, adjusted with administrative and physical controls. Darling recommends short process documents that name the people, procedures and technology behind each control, which keeps policies usable. He also shows how tiering internet-facing assets for faster remediation puts risk-based priorities into practice.

Compliance frameworks such as SOC 2 and ISO 27001 are presented as a way to communicate trust to customers, auditors and regulators. Darling suggests generating audit evidence from routine workflows, such as closed ticket records, and mentions OSCAL as a machine-readable option. He closes by arguing that compliance is a business competitiveness issue and should describe what the organization really does.

talks.title: Breaking Your Silence: Build Influence Without Becoming a "Suit"
talks.teaser: Shows security professionals how to share their expertise and build influence without self-promotion or corporate posturing.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a story from the speaker's early years in cybersecurity marketing, when she stayed quiet in meetings for a year until a suggestion about hosting customer dinners changed how her company worked. She argues that the industry rewards discretion, so quiet expertise often goes unnoticed, underfunded or misunderstood. Self-doubt, such as feeling an exploit is not impressive enough or that someone has already said it better, keeps many people from sharing their work.

The middle of the session walks through a five-part framework named Vela: foundation, which means moving from hesitation to action and challenging negative self-talk; narrative, which means connecting expertise to personal values and a clear one- or two-sentence story; signal, which means sharing ideas through high-value conversations rather than broadcasting; network, which means building a varied community instead of chasing follower counts; and system, which means setting focused goals and small daily habits. Low-risk entry points include co-presenting, contributing to group projects, commenting thoughtfully online, speaking at local chapter meetings, and joining podcasts. The speaker also suggests checking whether you have already reached a goal you are still chasing.

The closing message is that small repeated actions, such as pressing send on a draft or introducing yourself to one person, compound over time. Attendees were asked to name a belief holding them back and to consider why they had not acted on it. The takeaway for practitioners is that readiness rarely arrives on its own, and that deliberate, relationship-driven visibility can extend a career and create opportunities that technical work alone does not.

talks.title: The Interview Engine: A Career Readiness Framework
talks.teaser: Explains how security hiring works and offers a data-driven framework for staying career-ready.
talks.summary:
Vas Khomyk, a recruiter who has worked in cybersecurity and technology hiring for over a decade, opens by arguing that there is no silver bullet in hiring. He describes a market shaped by tighter budgets, job descriptions that bundle several roles into one, very high applicant volumes, and fabricated or impersonated candidates that hiring teams now have to screen for.

The middle of the talk covers how candidates actually get found. Recruiters search LinkedIn with Boolean queries and rank profiles by how often terms appear, so headlines, titles and wording matter. Referrals, conference visibility and open-source work often lead to placements faster than cold applications. Khomyk advises naming the problems you have solved instead of listing tools, dropping irrelevant early roles and keyword stuffing, and treating resume versions as experiments whose results you measure.

For the close, he presents an "interview engine" with three states: cold, idling and running. Work quality is the fuel, visibility to your network is the air, and active applying and interviewing is the spark. He recommends tracking your own application data, iterating on resume versions, and recording accomplishments every year so that a job search can restart quickly when it is needed.

talks.title: Alert Fatigue Is a Misdiagnosis
talks.teaser: Argues that alert fatigue is often misdiagnosed rather than simply caused by too many alerts.

talks.title: Flirting With AI: Pwning Web Sites Through Their AI Chatbot Agents
talks.teaser: Shows how chatbot agents on public websites can be coaxed into leaking client data through prompt manipulation and encoding tricks.
talks.summary:
Paul Brownridge opens by framing website AI chatbots as a new attack surface, with guardrails sitting in front of a language model much as a web application firewall sits in front of an application. He walks through public chatbot failures, from a drive-through order flood to a hiring bot exposed with weak default credentials, and argues that many LLM risks are familiar web flaws under new names. Prompt injection maps to input validation, unbounded consumption to missing rate limits, and excessive agency to over-privileged backends.

The middle of the talk covers case studies and a demonstration. A European rail operator's chatbot validated only the current session, so earlier chat history returned by its API could be manipulated, enabling indirect prompt injection and HTML injection that could lead to cross-site scripting. A March incident in which Morse code decoding was used to move a large sum of cryptocurrency is also discussed. The live demo targets a fictional, deliberately vulnerable legal-firm assistant built on Azure OpenAI with retrieval over blob storage. The speaker probes its boundaries, wraps requests in a legal pretext, asks for base64-encoded instructions, and resubmits prompts to get past refusals, eventually retrieving a confidential lease document through a storage link.

The closing advice is to test AI features regularly, build them with strict input handling from the start, and not assume a deployed model is foolproof. The field is immature, but the speaker argues it is a rich source of findings for assessors.

talks.title: 5-Step Method for Turning Security Findings Into Stories
talks.teaser: Shows how to reshape technical security findings into business-risk narratives that prompt executives to make a decision.
talks.summary:
Victoria Mosby opens with a common frustration: security teams write accurate reports that leaders acknowledge but rarely act on. She uses a fictional financial firm, Meridian Finance, and follows a CISO who must ask a chief financial officer for budget to remove standing administrator credentials left in two legacy directory forests. The request is politically sensitive because a similar fix was deferred in an earlier assessment, and peer firms have since been breached through the same weakness.

The core of the session is a five-step method. The presenter first reduces the request to one sentence that names the decision, the amount, the deadline and the stakes. Next she picks a narrative pattern from a framework she calls the saga model. She contrasts a "prophet's warning," which recounts an ignored finding and assigns accountability, with a "dragon's awakening," which presents the same facts as a current risk without blame. The remaining steps cover mapping the realm, the decision-makers and the proposed work, choosing how much story to add on a conservative-to-full-narrative scale, and checking that every metaphor still rests on verifiable data. She walks through a second example about replacing an end-of-service portfolio platform.

The takeaway is practical. Mosby asks attendees to apply the method to one finding before their next working day, present both the original and reframed versions to a stakeholder, and see which one gets a response. She stresses keeping numbers constant and avoiding jargon and theatrics.

talks.title: Catching Collection in M365: Outlook and SharePoint Canary Tokens
talks.teaser: Shows how canary messages and files in Outlook and SharePoint can flag attackers or insiders searching for data after token theft.
talks.summary:
Once a stolen token gives an attacker access to Microsoft 365, they often search mailboxes and file stores for valuable data before taking it. The speaker explored canary items placed where such searches land: messages in hidden Outlook folders and files in finance and HR areas of SharePoint. Alerts fire when those specific items are opened, using native Unified Audit Log events rather than another product. Tracking the internet message ID for mail and the list item unique ID for files keeps detection tied to the item itself instead of its subject or file name.

Two pilots ran in small business environments. The first deployed 50 Outlook canaries over three months and produced three alerts. One came from a departing employee who was collecting customer information for a new employer, showing that the same signal can catch insiders as well as external attackers. The second pilot added ten SharePoint files, but the team had removed invoice and wire lures to cut noise. A later business email compromise searched only for those removed terms, so no alert fired.

The main takeaways are that canaries detect collection whoever performs it, that filtering out lure terms is a bet on attacker intent, and that a baseline period before deployment helps tune noise. Mail sync events and file preview events proved too broad to rely on, and activity that never touches a canary goes unseen. Teams with limited tooling can still build useful detection from audit log data.

talks.title: When Your Target Runs On Attention Instead Of Anxiety
talks.teaser: Lays out a repeatable method for manipulating LLM agents by borrowing social engineering tactics like authority and pretext.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that prompt injection against language model systems is closer to social engineering than to classic memory-corruption bugs. Because models are trained to be helpful, they tend to comply with whoever sounds authoritative or sits closest to the end of their context, much as people do. The speaker explains why keyword filtering and input sanitising fall short, since natural language is too large a space to filter, and why permissions and intent checks have to sit outside the model.

The middle of the talk maps familiar social engineering ideas onto models. Reconnaissance becomes interrogating an agent to build a behaviour profile, pretexting becomes fabricating a shared history, and authority, urgency, reciprocity, cognitive overload and gradual rapport-building become prompt framings. Indirect injection through resumes, web forms, PDFs and tool output is treated as a form of retrieval poisoning. The speaker also describes a search-style workflow that generates, scores and mutates prompts, and notes that setting temperature to zero only makes a working attack repeatable rather than safer.

The closing point is that teams should treat model output as a suggestion rather than a decision, and should contain the blast radius of injection instead of expecting to prevent it. Practitioners testing these systems should record the model, settings and full context so results can be replayed and reported, and should be wary of prompt-based governance that adds complexity without adding real control.

talks.title: Building Custom Detections with Zeek and Spicy
talks.teaser: Shows how Zeek scripts and Spicy parsers can catch a Redis replication exploit that loads a malicious module.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Zeek, an open-source passive network monitor that watches a copy of network traffic from a span port or tap and turns it into compact logs covering many protocols. The speaker explains why those logs are useful both for live investigations and for looking back at older traffic without keeping full packet captures, and describes Zeek's event-driven scripting language.

The core example is a Redis remote code execution. An unauthenticated Redis server can be told to become a replica of an attacker's server, then receive a shared library disguised as a database sync and load it as a module, which gives the attacker command execution. The speaker walks through the Redis wire protocol and shows how Spicy, a parser generator for network protocols, turns raw bytes into structured units and raises events that Zeek can react to.

With those events available, the detection is a short Zeek script that checks each Redis command against an allow list and raises a notice when a disallowed command such as the module-loading one appears. The speaker also shows how the Redis log can be searched for unexpected commands and for an ELF file header appearing right after a full resync. The takeaway is that Zeek can flag this kind of exploit and supports custom logic beyond signature matching, although it is passive and does not block traffic itself.

talks.title: Community is a Control: Strengthening Cybersecurity Through Connection
talks.teaser: Argues that peer connections and team trust help security staff handle incidents and avoid burnout.
talks.summary:
Chelsea Bryan, a SOC analyst with four years at a university, opens by asking why security conversations focus so heavily on tools, detections and automation while the people doing the work are under-resourced and stretched thin. She describes what makes a team function: trust, communication, respect and a shared purpose. She argues that no tool or AI system replaces colleagues who can guide, check work and escalate when something breaks.

The middle of the talk covers building connections beyond one's immediate team. She points to mentorship programs, hobby groups and professional clubs such as Toastmasters, and explains how regular non-work conversations helped her recover from a stressful stretch. For incident response, she recommends clear leadership, split tasks, and writing after-incident reports and procedures together. She also lists local options in the Richmond area, including the monthly RVAsec meetup, the HackRVA space and a Women in Cybersecurity group she tried to start.

In audience questions, she advised someone in Savannah to begin with one motivated person and an online group, and advised managers to add mentorship, short team activities during the workday and better resources for analysts. Her takeaway is to treat community as a control: build it before an incident forces the need, and reach out to others when problems pile up.

talks.teaser: Covers how to protect AI systems and the training and operational data that feeds them.
